newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis talks await right environment - Fujimori.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis talks await right environment - Fujimori.

text.p: Peru's government will not resume direct talks with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages in Lima until it is confident of chances for real progress, President Alberto Fujimori said late on Sunday.
Fujimori's crisis negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, has not met with the leaders of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) for three weeks.
The Peruvian leader said Palermo would not go back to the negotiating table unless there were prospects that talks could move forward.

"Minister Palermo cannot go and bash heads with the MRTA, but rather (talk) in an environment in which we can say that we are making progress," Fujimori said in an interview with Peru's Panamericana television network.

The breakdown in direct talks has left a three-man mediation panel to carry out a kind of shuttle diplomacy between the government and the MRTA rebels holed up inside the Japanese ambassador's residence for 110 days.
But Fujimori denied reports that one of the mediators, Vatican representative Juan Luis Cipriani, had elevated negotiations to the MRTA's leadership.

Local media reported that Cipriani had visited a naval base in the port of Callao late on Friday where the MRTA's maximum leader Victor Polay and at least two other MRTA prisoners are serving life sentences.
But Fujimori said journalists had been misled by Cipriani's car, which took a church collegaue to collect a relative from the naval base.

A group of about 20 heavily-armed MRTA rebels stormed a cocktail party thrown by Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki on Dec. 17 and took more than 500 guests hostage. They released most of the hostages, but kept a group including Aoki, two Cabinet ministers, Fujimori's brother and the Bolivian ambassador.
Fujimori reiterated his pledge not to use force to end the 15-week standoff "unless there is an uncontrollable situation, in which there is a victim."
There was no sign that the MRTA had harmed any of the hostages, although many are reported to be suffering stress-related disorders after months in captivity.

"My father suffers from (high) blood pressure and has a heart problem, too, so we have always been worried about his health," Ana Teresa Pantoja, daughter of captive former Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja, told the America Television network.
Peru's firm stance against the hostage takers won plaudits on Sunday from two U.S. security experts during a discussion on the Cable News Network's Spanish language channel.

"We have to send a clear message to terrorists, rebels, criminals or guerrillas that the tactic of hostage-taking is wrong and does not work," said Michael Skol, a former State Department assistant secretary.
"There should be no concessions and one has to be prepared for a military action," said independent security expert William Perry.
But after nearly four months of fruitless efforts to end the siege, there were growing signs that Peruvians have become impatient with the way it is being handled.
A poll, conducted by consulting firm CPI and published in local newspaper El Comercio, showed that approval for Fujimori's management of the siege had fallen to 28 percent from 66 percent in January.

In the poll of 400 people in Lima and the neighbouring city of Callao, 20 percent of respondents said the government should give more ground to win a solution and 49 percent said the MRTA should do so. The poll did not give a margin of error.
There was little activity at the diplomatic site on Sunday, with Cipriani the only mediator to visit the residence.

Fellow mediator Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent later left for Bolivia where he told reporters he would meet with Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Losada to discuss the crisis as well as attending to routine diplomatic duties.
